Quirky: A recent Heise [article][article] covers how a Swiss student recreated 
Switzerland in Minecraft at 1:1 scale. From the [article][article]:

> A 22-year-old student at ETH Zurich thinks on a very small scale – literally: 
He has recreated Switzerland as an explorable Minecraft world. Rather than 
placing every block by hand, he generated the world automatically from official 
geodata. In the “Blocks” project, one block represents one meter, and the world 
covers the country’s entire area of 41,285 square kilometers.

The [project][project] uses mostly federal geodata: terrain data from swissALTI3D, 
limnology from swissBATHY3D, forest canopy and tree heights from swissSURFACE3D, 
building data from swissBUILDINGS3D, rock formations from GeoCover, several 
objects from the Swiss landscape model data product swissTLM3D and from 
SWISSIMAGE[^swissimage] 
aerial imagery and a few more data sources.

![The Lauterbrunnen Valley (which inspired Tolkien's Rivendell) in Minecraft (source: Manifold3D)](lauterbrunnen.jpg "The Lauterbrunnen Valley (which inspired Tolkien's Rivendell) in Minecraft (source: Manifold3D)")

Part of this model is accesible free of charge, part of it has a fee attached 
to it. Certainly one of the more "out there" uses of open geodata by 
Switzerland's public administration.

![The Eiger north face (source: Manifold3D)](eiger.jpg "The Eiger north face (source: Manifold3D)")

The [article][article] also points to [Manifold][manifold] (of which the 
Minecraft project is a subdomain), another project by the same author that 
offers custom extents of Switzerland converted to solids in the STL[^stl] format 
ready for 3D printing.

[article]: https://www.heise.de/en/news/Switzerland-recreated-at-1-1-scale-in-Minecraft-using-geodata-11500845.html
[project]: https://blocks.manifold3d.ch/
[manifold]: https://manifold3d.ch/

[^swissimage]: Consistency pet peeve: I feel this should be branded "swissIMAGE".
[^stl]: [STL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STL_(file_format)) (usually read as "stereolithography", sometimes "standard triangle/tessellation language") is a file format created in the 1980s for first commercial 3D printers. It describes the surface geometry of an object as a mesh of triangles, without colour, texture or units, and remains the de facto standard for 3D printing.
